content:
Major repair scaffolding increases the risk of burglaries in units. Some contractors, when erecting scaffolding that extends onto the pavement, have installed CCTV with cameras pointed at passers-by.

At least 11 buildings in Sham Shui Po and Cheung Sha Wan have CCTV installed on scaffolding, some filming the pavement

Many old buildings line the streets of Sham Shui Po and Cheung Sha Wan, where it is not uncommon to see scaffolding erected for repair works. Observations by Collective Insights recently found that at least 11 buildings in the area, currently undergoing major repair works, have closed-circuit television installed on their scaffolding, ranging from a single camera to as many as six. Some cameras only film the vicinity of the building entrances, while others capture back-alley conditions; however, many are pointed at the pavement, filming passers-by.

Scaffolding extending onto the pavement effectively means CCTV has been installed on the pavement itself.

Some buildings have notices posted at their entrances warning of CCTV surveillance.

Owners' corporation chair: burglaries occurred after scaffolding erected; CCTV installed for safety

Why is CCTV being installed on scaffolding? A worker carrying out works at a building on Cheung Sha Wan Road said the reason was to "prevent theft", explaining: "We're afraid people will climb up and steal things." At another building on Un Chau Street, which also has CCTV on its scaffolding, a notice posted in the stairwell states that two burglary cases involving residential units have already occurred since repair works began. The building's owners' corporation chairman, Mr Wan, said burglaries happened shortly after the scaffolding was erected, and "the construction company felt that, for safety's sake, they added some closed-circuit television".

Scaffolding extending onto the pavement means repair works have effectively resulted in CCTV being installed on the pavement itself.

CCTV successfully catches thief stealing lightning conductors

A building on Wong Chuk Street also has CCTV installed on its scaffolding. A staff member of the works contractor, Sing Kee Engineering, Mr Wu, revealed that since installation they have already "caught a thief": "A thief went up to steal the lightning conductors to sell them, but because there was CCTV, we could see the thief up there." He said that to ensure security during the building's repair works, installing CCTV to film the scaffolding area was standard practice: "To make sure that if any strangers or whoever climb onto the scaffolding, security will know immediately and go catch them."

A building on Wong Chuk Street also has CCTV installed on its scaffolding. A staff member of the works contractor, Sing Kee Engineering, Mr Wu, revealed that since installation they have already "caught a thief".

Most have not followed PCPD guidelines on notices; only one building has posted notices

According to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data's "Guidance on the Use of Closed-Circuit Television Monitoring", data users should clearly inform people who may be affected that they are subject to CCTV monitoring; one effective method is to display prominent notices within the monitored area. However, as observed by reporters on site, of the 11 buildings, four have only pre-existing notices at their entrances such as "CCTV filming in the vicinity" or "24-hour CCTV installed here", while six have no notices whatsoever at the building entrances or on the perimeter, including two buildings on Un Chau Street and Wong Chuk Street.

Only one building in Cheung Sha Wan, on Castle Peak Road, was found to have prominent notices posted within the monitored area, including on the scaffolding near the cameras. Some notices comply with the Guidance by specifying the data user's information, stating that the CCTV is managed by Cosmos (Group) Construction Limited and providing a contact number for enquiries about personal data handling.

Reporters inspected 11 buildings with CCTV installed in pavement areas; only one had prominent warning notices near the cameras

The company's Mr Chow, in response to enquiries, said the CCTV was installed out of concern that people might climb the scaffolding, to prevent trespassers and burglaries, giving police more information for investigations: "Actually, we just want to let thieves know it's not worth the trouble, to pick somewhere easier, not here." He said before installation, they had communicated with the building's owners' corporation, consultants, and the gold shop on the ground floor. The gold shop, which had experience with CCTV installation, reminded them that notices must be posted to inform the public, and the consultants gave similar advice: "We're worried people might mistake it for private use."

Most passers-by don't mind being filmed: "There's not much privacy on the street"

Passers-by going about their business may be captured by CCTV. Most did not notice the cameras but largely said they did not mind, though some felt posting notices was preferable. Mr Lee stated bluntly: "There's not much privacy on the street," and was not worried about privacy issues from CCTV. "It's perfectly normal; lots of shops have it." He thought having notices was good but without them, "they're not going to leave it up forever, so it's not an issue. Once the works are done, it'll be taken down."

Walking along the street, have you noticed you're already living under the gaze of CCTV cameras?

An elderly gentleman who declined to give his name also said: "There are more and more cameras now. Where is there any privacy, tell me?" Regarding the presence of cameras, he said as long as it's not illegal, he doesn't mind: "If you're breaking the law, of course you'd be afraid, of course it wouldn't be good!" But he added that some people simply do not wish to have their movements known. Ms Chan, a resident who frequently walks along Cheung Sha Wan Road, also had not noticed the CCTV on the scaffolding of one of the buildings, but said she did not mind: "No problem, it's for safety." She added: "At least if a thief catches me, there's footage." Ms Leung, who was passing by, also said she did not mind: "I'm only here for a minute, so they'll only film me for a minute!"

Some passers-by say notices would be better: "If you don't like it, you can take a detour"

Mr Ng held a different view: "Filming the gate area is actually OK, there's no need to film the whole street." However, he added that he was not a nearby resident and rarely passed by, so he was relatively unbothered. He agreed that having notices would be better: "At least you know there's a camera here, and you might be filmed. If someone really doesn't want to be filmed, they can take a detour."

During major repairs, some construction firms install CCTV for anti-theft purposes

Owners' corporation chair and contractor question: shops with CCTV also lack notices

Regarding CCTV filming passers-by without notices to inform them of surveillance, Mr Wan asked rhetorically: "Turning it around, many shops also have CCTV pointing onto the street — do they post notices? It seems they don't." He later said this issue would need to be looked into further.

Mr Wu similarly questioned whether notices were necessary: "CCTV everywhere films like this — shops, for instance, film like this too. No one says they have to post notices. You walk into any shop and you're being filmed like this; even the police use this to catch thieves!" He stressed that filming in public areas is permissible: "I don't prefer them doing whatever there, but we're just protecting our own." He also said that if requested, notices could be posted: "We don't mind; we're just protecting the owners' corporation and the service users."

PCPD reminds: purpose must be communicated; data subjects may request access

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner, in response to enquiries from Collective Insights, declined to comment on individual cases. The office reminded building owners or works contractors that if closed-circuit television systems with recording functions capable of capturing and storing images or footage of individuals — to be used for identifying those persons or compiling data on specific individuals — are installed on scaffolding, this may constitute the collection of "personal data" and must comply with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and its six data protection principles.

The office further noted that this includes requirements that personal data must be collected for a lawful purpose directly related to a function or activity of the data user, collected by lawful and fair means, and that all practicable steps must be taken to inform data subjects at or before the time of collection of the purposes for which the data will be used, the classes of persons to whom the data may be transferred, and the rights and channels through which data subjects may request access to and correction of their own data.

CCTV cameras are pointed at scaffolding at major repair sites for anti-theft purposes

Recording not enabled does not constitute collecting "personal data"; Privacy Ordinance does not apply

The office also reminded owners or contractors that, unless they have obtained the voluntary and explicit consent of data subjects, the use, disclosure, and transfer of personal data is limited to the purposes stated at the time of collection or purposes directly related thereto. As for CCTV that does not have recording functions enabled, the office stated that installing such systems does not involve the collection of "personal data", and the relevant provisions of the Privacy Ordinance do not apply.

Buildings under repair have CCTV installed on the pavement; some citizens see no issue, while others believe prominent warning notices should be posted

Lawyer: if it would impair detection of crime, exemption from notice requirements may apply

Solicitor Mr Chan Pak-ho told Collective Insights that the Privacy Ordinance requires that the method of collecting personal data should be notified to the data subject, for example, by posting notices informing them that CCTV is collecting images at the location. Failure to post notices may violate the data protection principles of the Ordinance. However, he also pointed out that in the context of preventing or detecting crime, if posting notices would impair that purpose, the Ordinance provides for an exemption: "Because once we post these notices, it may alert those intending to commit offences that they shouldn't commit them here but should do so elsewhere, which could undermine the purpose of detecting crime." He considered that in certain circumstances, installing CCTV without notices does not necessarily violate the data protection principles of the Ordinance.

Mr Chan pointed out that if the PCPD issues an enforcement notice to a building's management office requiring rectification of the breach of data protection principles within a specified period, failure to comply constitutes an offence punishable by fine and imprisonment. Regarding the placement of notices, he said posting at the building entrance would be sufficient, but the notice must clearly state that CCTV covers not only the entrance and lobby but the entire building — for example, that CCTV is installed on the scaffolding — to have a better chance of meeting legal requirements.

Some buildings have posted CCTV warning notices at their entrances

Lawyer reminds: avoid filming residents; high-definition filming of streets without notices may be unlawful

Mr Chan reminded building owners that if they wish to install CCTV on scaffolding, they should avoid filming the interiors of residential units in their own or other buildings, as this would clearly violate residents' privacy: "Of course I understand there may be practical difficulties — on one hand, wanting a clear view of the entire scaffolding situation, and on the other, worrying about filming residents' units. This does require very skilful adjustment of angles."

As for filming the street, Mr Chan noted that public areas are not private spaces, and it is reasonable to expect that people may not have high expectations of personal privacy. However, if the footage is of very high definition, caution is needed: "If it's very high definition, meaning that as people walk past on the street, their facial features are actually being collected by CCTV somewhere, and at the same time there is no relevant notice given to them, then this situation may violate the principles of data collection under the Ordinance."

Cameras made by "Zhejiang Dahua Technology Co., Ltd." are a popular brand for scaffolding CCTV, used by at least 8 of the 11 buildings. The company was placed on the US Department of Commerce's Entity List in 2019.

A car repair shop has also installed CCTV on the street, reportedly to deter police from issuing parking tickets.

CCTV pointed directly at areas where passers-by walk.
